mcqs.question: A user views the same image twice in one app session, and it was only cached on disk before the first view. What should happen after the first view to make the second view fast?
options: Nothing needs to change — disk cache reads are as fast as memory cache reads
The image should be re-downloaded from the origin server on the second view to ensure freshness
The disk cache should be cleared after every read to save storage
The image should be promoted into the memory cache after the disk hit, so the second view reads from memory instead of disk again
mcqs.explanation: Promoting a disk-cache hit into the faster memory cache is exactly what makes the next access to the same data faster — skipping this means paying disk I/O cost repeatedly even for data already cached. Disk reads are meaningfully slower than memory reads, re-downloading from origin defeats the purpose of caching at all, and clearing the disk cache after every read would eliminate its benefit entirely.

mcqs.question: What's the advantage of server-driven cache headers (ETag, If-None-Match) over pure time-based expiry for a large, rarely-changing image?
options: It allows a cheap conditional request that can confirm the cached copy is still valid without re-transferring the image body, unlike a TTL which either trusts the cache blindly or refetches the whole thing
It eliminates the need for any caching at all
It requires no server-side support, unlike time-based expiry
It guarantees the image will never need to be re-fetched again
mcqs.explanation: Conditional requests using ETags let the client confirm freshness with a small request that can return a 304 with no body if unchanged, avoiding both blind trust in a TTL and a wasteful full re-download — a genuine middle ground time-based expiry alone can't offer. This approach requires real server-side support, doesn't eliminate caching, and doesn't guarantee the image is permanently valid forever.

mcqs.question: A team applies the same cache invalidation strategy (a 24-hour time-based TTL) uniformly to a product catalog listing and a user's live cart total. What's the concern specifically with the cart total?
options: There is no concern — a 24-hour TTL is appropriate for all data types uniformly
The cart total's staleness tolerance is much lower than the catalog listing's, so trusting a 24-hour-stale cache risks showing a wrong total the user would notice immediately
TTL-based caching cannot be applied to cart data under any circumstances
The concern is purely a performance one, not a correctness one
mcqs.explanation: The right invalidation strategy depends on each data type's actual staleness tolerance — a product catalog can tolerate a generous TTL, but a cart total is exactly the kind of data a user would notice being wrong, making a long TTL a real correctness risk, not just a performance trade-off. TTL-based caching can technically apply to cart data, just with a strategy that fits its low tolerance for staleness, not a blanket 24-hour window borrowed from unrelated data.

mcqs.question: An app considers prefetching full-resolution images for every item in a long, rarely-scrolled list on the chance the user taps one. Is this a good prefetching decision?
options: Yes, prefetching is always beneficial regardless of prediction confidence or cost

No — this is a low-confidence prediction (most items likely won't be tapped) paired with a high cost (full-resolution images for many items), which is exactly the combination that disfavors prefetching
Yes, because prefetching only ever uses cached bandwidth that would otherwise go unused
No — prefetching should never be used for images under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: Prefetching decisions should weigh prediction confidence against cost; a low-confidence, high-cost prefetch like this one wastes significant bandwidth and battery on likely-wrong predictions, unlike a high-confidence, low-cost prefetch such as the next page of a feed the user is actively scrolling toward. Prefetching is not universally good or universally inappropriate for images — it depends on this specific confidence/cost trade-off.

mcqs.question: An app's disk cache has no size cap or eviction policy and has grown to several gigabytes after months of use. What's the standard fix?
options: Set an explicit size cap with an LRU eviction policy, which most platform caching libraries provide out of the box
Disable disk caching entirely and rely only on memory cache
Instruct users to manually clear the app's cache via device settings as the primary solution
Increase the device's available storage, since this is a hardware limitation
mcqs.explanation: A bounded cache with LRU eviction once a size cap is reached is the standard fix, and it's typically available directly from platform caching libraries rather than needing to be hand-rolled. Disabling disk caching sacrifices its real performance benefit, relying on manual user cleanup isn't a real fix, and this is a software configuration issue, not a hardware limitation.

mcqs.question: Users on limited cellular data plans complain that an app burns through their data allowance quickly. The app prefetches the next several feed pages unconditionally regardless of connection type. What's the fix?
options: Disable prefetching entirely across all connection types to eliminate the complaint
Check the actual connection type and throttle or disable aggressive prefetching on cellular by default, reserving it primarily for Wi-Fi
Increase the prefetch distance so pages load even further ahead, reducing the number of prefetch triggers
This complaint cannot be addressed without redesigning the entire feed architecture
mcqs.explanation: The actual mistake is treating all connections as equally cheap to speculate on — conditioning prefetch aggressiveness on connection type (aggressive on Wi-Fi, throttled on cellular) directly fixes the complaint without giving up prefetching's benefit entirely. Disabling it everywhere sacrifices a real UX win on Wi-Fi unnecessarily, and increasing prefetch distance would make the underlying problem worse, not better.
